title: From Complacency to Contenders: How Pochettino’s ‘Ant Work’ Transformed the USMNT
summary: When Mauricio Pochettino took over the U.S. men’s national soccer team in late 2024, he discovered a problem deeper than tactics or fitness: a culture of complacency. Players who were regulars on the squad seemed unexcited about the upcoming 2026 World Cup, which the U.S. would co-host. For Pochettino, an Argentine who played in the 2002 World Cup and later coached European giants like Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain, and Chelsea, this was baffling. In Argentina, he said, players are “desperate” to represent their country and treat every call-up as if it were their last. The U.S. job, despite its prestige and a record-high salary, was seen by many as a step down. The team had just been bounced from the 2024 Copa América, leading to the previous coach’s firing. With less than two years until the World Cup, Pochettino faced an unprecedented challenge: reset the roster and the mindset. He embarked on what he later called “the work of an ant”—a slow, meticulous process. Over 18 months and roughly a dozen camps, he evaluated more than 70 players, insisting that everyone compete equally regardless of experience or club stature. The early results were ugly. A string of defeats in early 2025—0-1 to Panama, 1-2 to Canada, 1-2 to Turkey, and a crushing 0-4 to Switzerland—made a deep World Cup run seem like a fantasy. Then, a dispute with star winger Christian Pulisic and other players over participation in pre-Gold Cup friendlies led to their exclusion from that tournament roster. Critics questioned his methods, but Pochettino remained steadfast. “When building toward something, the process may not always look pretty,” he said. Slowly, the team began to gel. New talents emerged, and the squad developed a fighting spirit reminiscent of Pochettino’s Argentine roots. That transformation is now on full display. The U.S. won Group D in the 2026 World Cup and has an advantageous path into the knockout rounds, starting with a match against Bosnia and Herzegovina on Wednesday in Santa Clara, California. Pochettino’s gamble—trading short-term stability for long-term cultural change—appears to be paying off. The sleeping giant may finally be stirring.
why_it_matters: The USMNT’s transformation from complacency to a competitive, gritty team on the world stage shows how deep cultural change can unlock potential—not just in sports, but in any group project. For a generation of American kids, seeing their team finally stir as a “sleeping giant” at a home World Cup could reshape the country’s soccer identity and prove that patience during a messy rebuild can lead to something special.

background_read: Mauricio Pochettino is a famous Argentine football manager known for his intense pressing style and for developing young players at Tottenham Hotspur in England. Before coaching the USMNT, he led top European clubs including Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain. The U.S. last hosted the men’s World Cup alone in 1994, but the 2026 edition will be the first with 48 teams, co-hosted with Canada and Mexico. The American team has never won a World Cup, though a new generation of players competing in top European leagues raised hopes before the disappointing 2024 Copa América performance.

Christian Pulisic, a winger who plays for AC Milan in Italy, is one of the most talented American footballers and was central to the team’s plans before his temporary exclusion from the squad. The U.S. hoped to build on a promising run at the 2022 World Cup, but the group-stage exit at the 2024 Copa América, a South American championship, led to the firing of previous coach Gregg Berhalter and the urgent hiring of Pochettino with the home World Cup looming.

perspectives.description: Supporters of Pochettino argue his demanding, equal-competition approach forced players to fight for their spots, which built the mental toughness the team lacked. The Group D win and strong knockout path are seen as proof that sacrificing short-term results for long-term cultural change can turn a talented but underwhelming squad into a genuine contender.

Critics point to the humiliating defeats in 2025 and the temporary sidelining of stars like Pulisic as reckless decisions that almost derailed the program. They worry that Pochettino’s rigid methods risk losing the locker room and that one good group stage doesn’t erase the damage done by a string of poor performances.

Observers note a pattern in Pochettino’s career of slow starts followed by strong turnarounds, similar to his early days at Tottenham. The USMNT’s transition mirrors many club rebuilds where a manager resets culture before results improve, but the unique pressure of a home World Cup shortens the timeline and makes the gamble far riskier than in a club setting.

The real test is whether this team can sustain its new mentality beyond the 2026 tournament, especially as hosting duties fade and key players age. If the US can reach a historic semifinal or final, it might permanently raise expectations and youth investment, but a quick exit would invite questions about whether the ant-like process was too slow for the stakes.
